column1: What is the core invariant underlying all hardware troubleshooting methodology?
column2: Every observable symptom traces back to a measurable, repeatable physical phenomenon—hardware failures exist in one of three domains: electrical discontinuity, logical state corruption, or timing violation.

column1: Why does a novice's 'random component swapping' approach fail compared to the expert's method?
column2: The expert uses hypothesis-driven testing: formulating a falsifiable hypothesis (e.g., 'SPI MISO has insufficient slew rate due to trace capacitance') and designing a targeted measurement to confirm/refute it, rather than randomly swapping parts hoping for accidental success.

column1: What physical phenomenon causes CMOS gate output ambiguity at voltage thresholds?
column2: Metastability—a window where output voltage hovers between logic high and logic low, causing downstream circuits to potentially interpret the signal inconsistently.

column1: How does hardware degradation fundamentally differ from software degradation?
column2: Hardware degradation is thermodynamically irreversible (electromigration, solder fatigue, electrolytic breakdown), while software degradation (logical corruption, bit flips) can be restored to a pristine state via re-flashing.

column1: State the Arrhenius relationship's practical implication for component failure rate.
column2: Reaction/failure rates approximately double for every 10°C increase in junction temperature.

column1: What does Black's equation predict in interconnect reliability?
column2: Electromigration failures as a function of current density and thermal exposure in conductive interconnects.

column1: Name and describe the three temporal regimes of the reliability 'bathtub curve.'
column2: 1) Infant mortality: early failures from manufacturing defects (bad reflow, contaminated epoxy, ESD damage). 2) Useful life: random failures from transient overstress (voltage spikes, latch-up, cosmic ray upsets). 3) Wear-out: cumulative damage reaching critical thresholds (e.g., solder joint fatigue).

column1: Why is burn-in testing performed on components before shipment?
column2: To accelerate latent manufacturing defects (infant mortality failures) into observable failures by operating components at elevated temperature and voltage, so defective units are caught before deployment.

column1: State Ohm's Law and describe its diagnostic significance as a 'trinity' relationship.
column2: V = IR (Voltage = Current × Resistance). Measuring any two of the three quantities allows the third to be derived, forming the foundation of all electrical troubleshooting measurement.

column1: Why can a clean time-domain square wave still cause EMI or signal integrity failures?
column2: It may harbor high-frequency harmonics invisible in the time domain but revealed via Fourier/FFT analysis, which can radiate interference or violate signal integrity budgets on high-speed differential pairs.

column1: What three invariant cost quantities drive the repair-vs-replace economic decision?
column2: 1) Fully-loaded technician labor cost per hour, 2) Replacement cost of the assembly, 3) Opportunity cost of downtime.

column1: What minimum oscilloscope memory depth is specified for capturing intermittent hardware glitches, and why does it matter?
column2: 10 Mpts memory depth per channel—deeper memory permits capture of infrequent glitches within long acquisition windows, which is critical for diagnosing intermittent faults.
